unstyled/demo1.text: Here's a strange fact about calculus. There is a function that, at every single point, has a slope exactly equal to its own height. When it's at height five, it's climbing at a rate of five. When it's at height a thousand, it's climbing at a rate of a thousand. That function is e to the x, and today we're going to see why this isn't a coincidence or a trick. It's the whole reason the number e exists. Let's start with what a derivative actually measures. It tells you how fast a function is changing at a given moment. Take any exponential function, say two to the x. To find its slope, we compare its value at x with its value a tiny step later, at x plus h, and divide the change by h. The change is two to the x plus h, minus two to the x. Now here's the key move. Two to the x plus h is the same as two to the x times two to the h. So we can factor out two to the x, and the slope becomes two to the x, multiplied by the quantity two to the h minus one, all over h. Look at what just happened. The slope of two to the x is two to the x itself, times a leftover piece that depends only on h, not on x. As h shrinks toward zero, that leftover piece settles down to a fixed number. For base two, it's about 0.693. So the derivative of two to the x is roughly 0.693 times two to the x. It's proportional to itself, but not equal. Try base three, and the same pattern appears. The slope is three to the x times a constant, but this time the constant is about 1.099. Every exponential function has this property: its slope is always some constant multiple of its own value. That's what makes an exponential an exponential. The bigger it gets, the faster it grows, in perfect proportion. Now the constant for base two is less than one, and for base three it's more than one. So somewhere between two and three, there must be a base where that constant is exactly one. At that base, the leftover piece disappears, and the slope equals the function itself. That special base is e, approximately 2.718. In other words, e isn't defined as a mysterious number that happens to have a nice derivative. It's defined as the base that makes the growth constant exactly one. There's another way to see this, through money. Suppose you put one dollar in a bank that pays one hundred percent interest per year. If it's compounded once, you end with two dollars. Compound twice, and you get two point two five. Compound monthly, and you get about two sixty-one. Keep compounding more and more often, and the total creeps toward a limit, and that limit is e. So e is what you get when growth feeds on itself continuously, with every bit of new growth immediately starting to grow too. We can use this to check the derivative. The function e to the x can be written as the limit of one plus x over n, all raised to the power n, as n gets huge. Take the derivative of that expression. The power rule brings down the n, and the chain rule multiplies by one over n. Those cancel, leaving one plus x over n, raised to the power n minus one. And as n grows large, that is essentially the same expression we started with. The derivative of e to the x turns back into e to the x. One more perspective, for anyone who likes patterns. e to the x can be written as an infinite sum: one, plus x, plus x squared over two, plus x cubed over six, and so on, where each term is x to a power divided by that power's factorial. Now differentiate each term. The derivative of x is one. The derivative of x squared over two is x. The derivative of x cubed over six is x squared over two. Every term turns into the one before it, so the whole sum reproduces itself, just shifted over by one place. Since the sum goes on forever, nothing is lost. The result is the same series we started with. So three different routes lead to the same place. Algebra shows that exponentials have slopes proportional to themselves, and e is the base where the proportion is one. Compound interest shows e as the limit of growth building on growth. And the infinite series shows each term feeding the next in a perfect loop. That's why e to the x shows up everywhere: in population growth, radioactive decay, cooling coffee, and electrical circuits. Whenever the rate of change of something depends on how much of it there is, e to the x is hiding in the answer. Its derivative equals itself because that is exactly what it was built to do.

unstyled/demo2.text: Here's a strange fact: a chart can be completely accurate, with every number correct, and still leave you believing something false. Numbers don't lie on their own. But people can arrange them so they mislead. Today I'll show you the most common tricks, and the questions that catch them. Let's start with the classic: the truncated axis. Imagine a bar chart comparing two products. One scores 96, the other scores 98. If the vertical axis starts at 95 instead of zero, the second bar looks more than three times taller. Same data, dramatic difference. So the first thing to check is where the axis begins. For bar charts especially, bars should start at zero, because the height of the bar is supposed to represent the whole quantity. Line charts can sometimes zoom in legitimately, but even then, ask yourself whether the zoom is exaggerating something small. The second trick is the cherry-picked time window. Say a politician claims, "Crime has fallen every month since March." That may be true, but if crime spiked in February and March, you're just watching a return to normal. Pick a different starting point and the same data tells the opposite story. Whenever you see a trend, ask: why does the chart start here, and what happened before? Stretch the timeline in your mind. Third, watch for percentages without a base. "Risk doubles!" sounds terrifying. But if a risk goes from one in ten thousand to two in ten thousand, that's a hundred percent increase, and still almost certainly nothing to worry about. Relative change feels huge when the starting number is tiny. Always ask for the absolute numbers: doubled from what, to what? Fourth, the slippery word "average." If ten people are in a room and each earns fifty thousand dollars, then a billionaire walks in, the average income shoots up to nearly ninety million. Nobody in the room got richer, except one person. The mean is dragged around by extreme values; the median, the middle value, is far more representative. When someone says "average" about incomes, house prices, or anything lopsided, ask which average, and whether the median is available. Fifth, correlation dressed up as causation. Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. Hot weather drives both. Charts love to put two lines side by side and invite you to assume one pushes the other. Before you accept it, ask whether a third factor could explain both, whether the direction might be reversed, or whether it's just coincidence. With enough data, bizarre pairs of things line up by pure chance. Sixth, dual axes. A chart with one line measured on the left side and another on the right can be tuned so the two lines look perfectly synchronized. By changing the scale of either axis, the designer can make almost any two lines appear to move together, or diverge. If you see two different scales on one chart, be suspicious, and check what each axis actually says. Seventh, the sample. A survey says "90 percent of customers are satisfied." Who was asked? If only people who finished the whole purchase were surveyed, the unhappy ones already left. If five people were asked, then 90 percent isn't even possible. Look for how many people were surveyed, how they were chosen, and who might be missing. A big, random sample is trustworthy. A self-selected online poll is not. Eighth, visual distortion. Sometimes a graphic uses icons, like a small money bag and a big money bag, to represent values. If one value is twice the other, and the designer doubles both the height and the width, the area becomes four times larger. Your eye reads area, not height, so the difference looks exaggerated. Similarly, 3D pie charts make slices at the front look bigger than they are. And if the slices of a pie chart don't add up to a hundred percent, something is wrong. Finally, there's what's left out: missing labels, no source, no units, no mention of how the data was collected. A chart that doesn't tell you where its numbers came from is asking for trust it hasn't earned. So here's a quick checklist you can run in about ten seconds. Check the axes: where do they start, and are they consistent? Check the time frame: is it fair, or conveniently chosen? Check the comparison: are these absolute numbers or just percentages? Check the measure: mean, median, or something else? Check the source and the sample: who collected this, and who was counted? And check the claim: does the chart show correlation while the headline says cause? You don't need to be a statistician. You just need a habit of asking, "What would I need to see to be fooled, or not fooled, by this?" Do that, and numbers go from something that persuades you to something you can actually use.
